content: The studies reviewed had follow-up durations ranging from 4 to 25 years. The association between physical activity (PA) and cancer incidence was examined in adults, with detailed evidence provided in supplementary materials. Systematic reviews assessed the credibility of evidence, including the number of studies, study designs, and participant numbers. For liver cancer, six studies (median baseline age of 45 years, range 20–93 years) found no serious risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, or imprecision. However, the evidence was rated as low due to limitations in study design. For melanoma risk, three prospective cohort studies (12,605 cases) and five case-control studies (1,295 cases) were analyzed. Most studies focused on recreational PA. No serious inconsistency or indirectness was noted, but there was a serious risk of bias. Similarly, for prostate cancer, 48 prospective cohort studies and 24 case-control studies (151,748 cases) were reviewed. While no serious risk of bias or indirectness was identified, there was serious inconsistency and imprecision, with possible publication bias. The mean participant age was 61 years, and all studies relied on self-reported PA. No significant differences were observed when stratifying by study design (cohort vs. case-control). For lung cancer, 20 prospective cohort studies (31,807 cases) found a significant inverse relationship between higher PA levels and lung cancer risk. The evidence was rated as moderate, with no serious risk of bias, indirectness, or imprecision, but serious inconsistency and possible publication bias were noted. Regarding type 2 diabetes (T2D), 27 prospective cohort studies (1,150,574 participants) examined the relationship between PA and T2D incidence across racial/ethnic groups. Follow-up durations ranged from 2 to 28 years, with diabetes ascertainment methods varying (e.g., medical records, medication use, oral glucose tolerance tests, fasting blood glucose, or self-report). Higher PA levels were associated with reduced diabetes risk. However, studies among South Asian adults (three cross-sectional studies, 14,902 participants) found no association between total PA and T2D incidence. The evidence was rated as very low due to serious bias, indirectness, and imprecision. For adiposity-related outcomes, studies examined the relationship between PA and measures of adiposity (e.g., BMI, waist circumference, fat mass). Light-intensity PA (LIPA) showed favorable associations with waist circumference in 8 out of 12 cross-sectional studies but inconsistent associations with BMI. One cohort study found that women in the highest tertiles of LIPA had lower fat mass and central fat compared to those in the lowest tertiles. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) was compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) in 48 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or pre-post studies (1,222 participants). HIIT was associated with reductions in body weight but showed no significant differences compared to MICT for BMI, waist circumference, or body fat percentage. For mental health outcomes, studies evaluated the effects of PA on anxiety and depression. Exercise interventions lasting 6–12 weeks were associated with reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression among middle-aged and older women. Resistance training was also found to significantly reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression in RCTs, with intervention durations ranging from 11 to 16 weeks. Most studies relied on self-reported PA, and the evidence was rated as moderate due to possible publication bias and variability in study designs. In summary, while PA is generally associated with favorable health outcomes, the strength of evidence varies across outcomes and populations, with limitations such as bias, inconsistency, and reliance on self-reported data affecting the certainty of findings.
